stories.headline: Lakewood police agent killed, three officers wounded in shootout at RTD bus stop on West Colfax
stories.summary:
A Lakewood Police Department agent was killed and three other officers were wounded Thursday night in a shootout with a man who tried to board a Regional Transportation District bus at West Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard. The suspect was also killed. A civilian was injured as well, according to authorities.

Police said officers responded at about 6:30 p.m. to a report of a suspicious person attempting to board the bus. Another account said an agent had pursued the suspect of a hit-and-run who was seen boarding the bus. When officers made contact, the man opened fire and a firefight followed.

The wounded officers were taken to area hospitals, including Denver Health, and their conditions had not been publicly released. A procession was held Thursday night in honor of the fallen agent. The Lakewood Police Department held a news conference on the shooting, and the investigation is continuing.

stories.headline: Colorado congressional delegation could turn bluer as two Republican incumbents lose and a third trails
stories.summary:
Colorado's 4-4 split in its U.S. House delegation was upended this week as two Republican congressmen lost their seats. Democrat Manny Rutinel defeated Rep. Gabe Evans in the 8th District, and the Associated Press called the 5th District for Democrat Jessica Killin over Rep. Jeff Crank, marking the first Democratic win in that El Paso County-centered district.

In the 4th District, Rep. Lauren Boebert trailed Democrat Eileen Laubacher by fewer than 3,500 votes Wednesday evening, and the race had not been called as of Thursday afternoon. In the 3rd District, Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd held a thin but growing lead over Democrat Dwayne Romero.

State Democratic Party Chair Shad Murib said the party has not given up on winning all eight seats. Democratic strategist Andy Boian predicted a 7-1 delegation. Colorado has not sent a single-party House and Senate slate to Washington since 1941.

stories.headline: Weiser and Democrats plan changes to approved ballot measures on fentanyl and transgender youth
stories.summary:
Governor-elect Phil Weiser and leading Democrats in the legislature are discussing how to alter four conservative ballot measures that appear to have passed. They are Propositions 132 on fentanyl penalties, 133 on child sex trafficking, 134 on school sports and 135 on gender-affirming surgery for minors.

The measures are statutory and can be changed or repealed by a simple legislative majority. Democrats are expected to hold supermajorities in both chambers, with projections of 24-11 in the Senate and 49-16 in the House.

Weiser said Wednesday the state would need to look at what adjustments are necessary and appropriate, and said he does not think it is acceptable for every young athlete to be checked for their biological sex. He offered no specifics, and options range from full repeal to minor changes. The Associated Press had not yet called Propositions 132 and 135.

stories.headline: Colorado voters pass Proposition NN, raising TABOR cap by $4.6 billion for K-12 education
stories.summary:
Colorado voters approved Proposition NN, which raises the TABOR cap on government growth by $4.6 billion, equal to the highest amount the state has previously spent on education. The money, which would otherwise be refunded to taxpayers, is earmarked for K-12 schools.

State Sen. Jeff Bridges, now treasurer-elect, authored the measure and called it the most impactful thing he could have done as a legislator. Colorado Education Association President Kevin Vick said the money could lower class sizes, raise teacher pay and expand career and technical education.

TABOR author Douglas Bruce said state law cannot override the constitution and predicted possible court challenges. Amendment 87, which would create a graduated income tax, appeared poised to pass narrowly.

stories.headline: Metro Denver home sales volume falls by a quarter as buyers and sellers pull back
stories.summary:
The dollar value of homes sold in metro Denver dropped from $2.62 billion in October 2025 to $1.97 billion last month, according to the Denver Metro Association of Realtors. Closings fell 8.6% on the month and 23.5% on the year, to levels not seen since October 2010.

Pending sales fell 7.3% from September and are down 20.3% from a year ago. Mortgage rates briefly reached 7.5% on 30-year loans last month. DMAR's Amanda Snitker said fear influenced decisions on both sides of the market.

Median single-family prices rose 1.57% over the month to $645,000, and condo and townhome prices rose 2.74% to $375,000. Active listings fell 4.3% to just under 13,000.

stories.headline: Denver Rescue Mission to lay off 71 employees after city contract for 48th Avenue Center ends
stories.summary:
The Denver Rescue Mission will lay off 71 employees on Dec. 31 after its city contract to operate the 48th Avenue Center was terminated, according to a notice filed with the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment on Oct. 30. The shelter at 4600 E. 48th Ave. provides beds for 538 men, along with meals and other services.

CEO Dennis Van Kampen said the nonprofit chose not to bid on a new contract as it shifts toward programs that prevent homelessness. A city Department of Housing Stability spokeswoman said there will be no interruption to services and that a committee will discuss 2027 provider contracts Tuesday.

The mission will keep operating its Lawrence Street Shelter, The Crossing, and other facilities. Its school-based prevention pilot has kept 106 families in their homes.

stories.headline: Denver restaurants named among best in U.S. by OpenTable
stories.summary:
OpenTable named seven Denver restaurants to its Top 100 Restaurants in America list, up from five a year ago and matching the total for all of Texas. The list is based on more than 11 million verified diner reviews and other metrics, and includes only restaurants that use OpenTable.

Honorees include Johnny Curiel's Alma Fonda Fina, Mezcaleria Alma, Milpero and Alteño, along with The Wolf's Tailor, Colorado's only two-star Michelin restaurant. Guard & Grace and Florence Supper Club also made the list.

OpenTable's list is not ranked, and it described Denver as on the rise nationally.

stories.headline: National Western Stock Show adds skijoring to 2027 lineup
stories.summary:
The National Western Stock Show announced it will add skijoring to its 2027 schedule. In the sport, a horseback rider tows a skier on a rope through a course of rings, jumps and gates, with penalties for misses.

Fifty teams will compete in the inaugural invitational on Monday, Jan. 18, 2027, along Betty Cram Drive on the west side of the grounds, between The Legacy and the CSU Spur buildings. Organizers will begin making snow in late November.

Tickets start at $31 for adults and $10 for children.

stories.headline: Denver nonprofit Team HWH doubles its space to train more people facing housing instability
stories.summary:
Team Housed, Working & Healthy, a Denver nonprofit, held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new Swansea facility twice the size of its previous space. Its three-month culinary training program is a path out of housing instability.

Executive Director Brad Volin said the organization can now serve up to 200 people a year and has had a waitlist for years. The city of Denver committed $1.5 million, and a partnership with Brookdale Senior Living guarantees jobs for 25 graduates each year.

Graduate Geo Roberts is now a kitchen lead at Tokyo Joe's after starting at Ball Arena. The site is four blocks from the A line.

stories.headline: Denver Waymo pricing nearly matches Uber and Lyft, Gazette analysis finds
stories.summary:
The Denver Gazette recorded prices for Waymo, Uber and Lyft over a week, Sept. 25 to Oct. 1, at five times each day along routes across Waymo's Denver service area. Waymo's average price fell between its rivals, and its median was nearly the lowest of the three.

Waymo's prices were also more consistent, varying about half as much as Uber's and Lyft's. Its 6 a.m. Union Station to Capitol Hill fare ranged only from $11.45 to $14.05. When Waymo prices did jump, the increase was large, including a ride from Washington Park to Mission Ballroom that exceeded $60.

Waymo opened to waitlisted customers Sept. 1, and its operating fleet has grown from dozens to more than 100 vehicles.

stories.headline: Broncos rally past Chiefs 28-24 at Empower Field
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos came back from behind in the fourth quarter to beat the Kansas City Chiefs 28-24 at Empower Field at Mile High on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Linebacker Alex Singleton discussed the Week 8 win, and running back RJ Harvey was placed on injured reserve.

The Broncos next turn to Week 9 as the NFL trade deadline approaches.

topStory.headline: Federal Judge Temporarily Blocks Construction of Trump's Triumphal Arch Within an Hour of Planning Commission Approval
topStory.summary:
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan late Thursday issued a temporary restraining order barring the Trump administration from beginning construction on the planned 250-foot "Triumphal Arch" in Washington for 14 days. The order, which prohibits the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation" or related steps, came within an hour of the National Capital Planning Commission's 8-4 vote to approve final site and building plans. The four dissenting votes came from commissioners who were not appointed by President Trump.

In a 33-page ruling, Chutkan wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing the federal government did not follow required legal processes before moving to build the arch. She found that the District of Columbia and Virginia, which sued over the project along with a group of Vietnam veterans, likely have standing because of "tangible economic harms" tied to traffic problems at the construction site. Chutkan wrote that "the harm is certain," noting the administration had said it was ready to begin work almost immediately after approval. The Justice Department said in a court filing last month that construction could start as soon as Thursday, and a separate filing Wednesday said a construction company "may be" arranging off-site preparations.

The commission acted after a hearing in which public comment lasted more than nine hours, with close to 130 people signed up to speak. The virtual meeting was interrupted for about 30 minutes by what commission Chair Mark Paoletta described as a "malicious attack" that crashed the site. Paoletta, general counsel at the Office of Management and Budget and chairman of the commission since August, called it a "national disgrace" that such a memorial had not been built and said it would be "the grandest arch ever built by mankind." He and other commissioners said the project fulfills a 100-year plan for a monumental work on Columbia Island and would give Arlington National Cemetery a "monumental gateway."

Opponents focused on the arch's effect on Arlington National Cemetery, as well as its height, scale and safety. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said the project is "illegal" and argued that Congress is the appropriate body to debate such a monument. Marine veteran Jimi Shaughnessy criticized the prospect of a "carnival-like atmosphere of tourists, food trucks and buses." Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., whose district includes the cemetery, praised the ruling but said courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards. Veteran Anne Wright told the BBC she would try to stop construction, saying protesters would "tie ourselves to the bulldozer."

The arch, nicknamed the "Arc de Trump," is intended to commemorate the nation's 250th anniversary and is part of Trump's broader effort to reshape the capital. Renderings show a golden, winged Lady Liberty atop the structure, flanked by two gold eagles, with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed on its sides. The administration has also said the arch would double as a complex for storing military equipment, with the ability to deploy snipers and drones. The Department of the Interior and National Park Service did not immediately respond to requests for comment. With multiple lawsuits pending, it remains unclear when, or whether, construction will begin once the 14-day restraining order expires.
